title: Genomes from 10th-century conqueror cemeteries
fact_summary: Genetic studies of 10th-century graves in the Carpathian Basin find that most people were local, while an immigrant group carried ancestry the authors call Mansi-like, alongside Sarmatian and other components.

place.label: Great Hungarian Plain
place.note: Pin placed by Claude in the middle of the region the study names ('the Great Hungarian Plain'). It is not the position of any one grave.

claims.text: Maróti and colleagues sequenced 113 samples from the Hungarian conquest period, 48 of them from 10th-century cemeteries of the conquering Hungarian elite.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: They report that “the majority of the individuals from each period were local residents”.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: They model their core immigrant group (Conq_Asia_Core1) as about 50% Mansi and 35% Early or Late Sarmatian ancestry, with the rest from Scytho-Siberian, Xiongnu or Hun-related sources.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: They date the Mansi–Sarmatian mixture to about 53 generations before these people died, and a Mansi–Scythian/Hun-related mixture to about 24 generations before, which they give as 217–315 CE.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: An earlier study found that 7% of the conqueror elite carried the paternal lineage N1a1a1a1a4-M2118 and 10% carried N1a1a1a1a2-Z1936, “both of which are present in Ugric speaking Khantys and Mansis”.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: That study sampled 49 individuals “supposed to represent the power/military elit[e]”, and described the conquerors as “a recently assembled population incorporating un-admixed European, Asian as well as admixed components”.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: The conquering Hungarians had Ugric ancestry and later mixed with Sarmatians and Huns.
claims.certainty_reason: Argued with evidence in one tier B study, supported by paternal lineages reported by the same group. No review has been checked.

claims.text: The group the conquerors' ancestors mixed with “could be identified with ancestors of European Huns”. The authors note that medieval Hungarian chronicles and folk tradition claim descent from the Huns, but they themselves word the genetic link only as a possibility.
claims.certainty_reason: The authors themselves word it as a possibility ('could be identified').

claims.text: A 2021 study of maternal lineages from ordinary 10th–11th-century cemeteries found that these people differ significantly from the elite and group with European populations.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: A 2025 study with new genomes from the Urals finds that many 10th-century Hungarians share long DNA segments with people buried in the southern Urals in the 8th–10th centuries.

sources.locator: Results, “Early Medieval Magyars Fall within the Genetic Diversity of the Volga-Ural Region”

claims.certainty_reason: This records what the study reports, read in the open copy linked under Sources.

claims.text: The reference groups of the 2022 study (“modern Mansis, early/late Sarmatians, and Xiongnu”) are poor stand-ins for the conquerors' ancestors; groups from the Ural region itself are “much closer to the actual sources”.
claims.certainty_reason: A criticism of method made in one tier B study. No reply from the criticised group has been read.

dating_methods.text: The cemeteries are assigned to the 10th century by the study. How each grave was dated has not been checked here.
The mixture dates are worked out from the genomes themselves, counted in generations before death (a genetic method, not a calendar record).
dating_methods.certainty_reason: One tier B study; the method has not been checked against other work.

open_questions.text: The first studies sampled mostly elite graves. A 2021 study of maternal lines from ordinary cemeteries now exists (see the linked card); whole genomes from those cemeteries are still to be read.
How should a genetic ancestry share be read against the language the conquerors spoke?

review.note: Checked by Claude against open copies of every source. Marc spot-checks a sample.

contradictions.what_differs: How to describe the conquerors' eastern ancestry. The 2022 study reads it as Ugric ancestry later mixed with Sarmatians and Huns, using living Mansi and ancient Sarmatian and Xiongnu groups as references. The 2025 study rejects those references and derives the same people from early medieval groups of the southern Urals.

change_notes.note: Added a 2025 study that disputes the reference groups used here, shown as a contradiction, and a 2021 study that speaks to the open question about ordinary people.
